I have twelve mu of good flat land here in Quzhou, and I’ve been farming it for over thirty years. With my university background, I keep records and calculate my input rates rather than just guessing, but I also know that in this county, the wheat-maize double-cropping system is the only reliable way to make a living—anything else is gambling with the market and the weather. 

This year I will plant winter wheat on all twelve mu in mid-October. I’ll use an improved semi-dwarf variety that I bought from the county seed station; the germination rate is certified and it resists stripe rust better than the old local lines. For soil prep, I’ll run the rotary tiller twice to break up the maize stubble and incorporate the residue—no-tillage might save fuel, but wheat needs a firm, fine seedbed to survive the winter. I’m targeting 520 kg per mu for the wheat, which is realistic given the soil fertility here. To hit that, I’ll apply 22 kg of pure nitrogen per mu, split as 10 kg at basal plus 12 kg topdressed at jointing, plus 8 kg P₂O₅ and 5 kg K₂O at planting. Irrigation is expensive with the tube-well meter, but wheat cannot skip water in the spring—so I’ll irrigate four times: overwinter water, green-up, jointing, and grain-filling. I also budget four pesticide applications: one pre-emergence herbicide, one broadleaf herbicide in spring, and two fungicide/insecticide sprays at flag-leaf and heading to keep Fusarium and aphids under control.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I have about five days to get the maize in the ground. I will plant a hybrid summer maize variety with a 105-day maturity—no time for tillage, so I’ll use no-tillage direct seeding with a hired precision planter. I expect 580 kg per mu if the summer rains cooperate. The maize needs 18 kg N per mu, all applied at the V6 stage because the wheat already left residual phosphorus and I see no need to waste money on P and K for the short summer crop. I’ll irrigate twice, at the big-flush stage and at filling, because two good irrigations usually outperform three light ones on this soil. Three pesticide rounds will cover it: a pre-emergence atrazine mix, one post-emergence nicosulfuron application for grassy weeds, and one insecticide at the silk stage for corn borers.

I know I’m pushing the nitrogen a bit above county average, but I can afford it and the yield response is consistent on my fields. The biggest risk is still the summer drought during maize pollination, so I keep a cash reserve for an extra irrigation if July turns dry.
